## Part A
```{r}
# TODO: Question #1 - Create a vector with names
scores <- c(Ana = 78, Ben = 92, Cid = 85, Dex = 92, Eli = 67, Fay = 88, Gio = 74)
print(scores)

# TODO: Sort the scores in ascending and descending order
sort_asc <- sort(scores)
sort_desc <- sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE)
print(sort_asc)
print(sort_desc)

# TODO: Check whether the names stayed attached to their sorted values
names(sort_asc)

# TODO: Create subjects and incomplete vectors with missing values
subjects <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "PE")
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)

# TODO: Sort subjects alphabetically
sort(subjects)

# TODO: Sort incomplete using default sort() and with na.last = TRUE
sort(incomplete)
sort(incomplete, na.last = TRUE)

# TODO: Question #4 - Use order(scores) and compare to sort(scores)
order_res <- order(scores)
print(order_res)
scores[order_res]

# TODO: Question #5 - Create a data frame from vectors and reorder by score
students <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio"),
  score = c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74),
  section = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")
)
print(students)

# Reorder entire data frame by score ascending and descending
students[order(students$score), ]
students[order(students$score, decreasing = TRUE), ]

# TODO: Question #8 - Use rank(scores) and compare side by side
cbind(scores, Rank = rank(scores))

# TODO: Question #8 (Sales Challenge) - Create sales data frame, add rank, and reorder
sales <- data.frame(
  employee = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"),
  units_sold = c(120, 145, 145, 98, 130)
)
sales$rank <- rank(-sales$units_sold) # Top seller gets rank 1
sales[order(sales$units_sold, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```
Answers:
Question #2 

Yes, the names stayed with their numbers. If the names didn't move with the scores, all our grades would get mixed up and we would give the highest score to the wrong person.

Question #3 

Removing missing data without telling us is dangerous because it can hide data collection mistakes. If I was looking for the lowest score, R might ignore the missing data and give me the wrong impression of the results.

Question #4 

order() doesn't show the actual values; it just gives you the index numbers telling you where the values belong. When I put that inside scores[order_res], it rearranged the scores to match what sort() does.

Question #5 

I combined our vectors into a table (data frame). Using order() inside the brackets let me sort the whole table by score without messing up the rows or columns.

Question #6

order() just spits out a bunch of row position numbers (like 5, 1, 3). On its own, those numbers are just coordinates and don't mean anything unless you use them to rearrange a table.

Question #7 

You can't use sort() on a whole table because a data frame has multiple columns and rows, and R doesn't know which column to sort by. order() is better because it figures out the correct row order so all the other columns stay lined up together.

Question #8

Ben and Dex both got a rank of 6.5 because they tied for the highest score. R handles ties by taking the average of the positions they would have taken if they didn't tie.

Question #9

No, order() only gives you positions for sorting, not actual rankings or standings. We needed rank() to assign actual numerical placements and handle the ties properly.
